prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: I moved B006 from third to first after rereading the openings. The scientific case rests on three points. First, it joins a conceptual framework (tasks, skill demand, the race between education and technology) with credible quasi-experimental evidence on import competition and local labour markets. Second, the work is mature: the skill-premium line is about three decades old, the task framework over twenty years, and the China-shock papers over a decade, with replication, refinement and critique across countries. Third, the work changed how researchers and policymakers analyse distribution and adjustment costs. Attribution is imperfect but workable. Autor links the task and trade-shock strands, Hanson anchors the trade-shock design, and Katz anchors the long-run skill-premium and education-technology literature. The B004 case is also very strong on influence and maturity, but its attribution is diffuse. Eight credited names and no clean three-person cut make a B004 prize more contestable on who made the discovery. B001 has clearer credit within the core trio, but the legal-origins identification critiques weigh on its confirmation. My earlier B004-first ranking reflected the importance of the framework, not a view that attribution is easy.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The task framework has important contributors outside this entry (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu). Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is left out only by the three-person cap. Katz's education-technology work overlaps with the work of a recent laureate (Goldin), and the technology and inequality agenda is adjacent to the 2023 and 2024 prizes, so the marginal discovery recognised here needs a clear statement. The magnitude and persistence of trade-shock effects, and the shift-share inference concerns, are still debated. Technology and trade may be two strands rather than one discovery.

responses.point: Friberg proposes only Autor and Hanson for B006. He sees Autor as central to both the task framework and the trade-shock work, and Hanson as central to the import-competition evidence. He treats Katz and Dorn as adjacent, and notes that Acemoglu's earlier recognition touches task theory.
responses.response: A two-name prize centred on the China shock and tasks is coherent and avoids the Katz-versus-Dorn dilemma. I still keep Katz. The skill-premium and education-technology framework is a distinct, long-validated achievement. It supplies the supply-and-demand account into which the task and trade-shock evidence fits, and without it the citation covers only the later empirical strand. I accept that this makes the citation broader and the Goldin overlap more delicate, which is why I keep it as an open question for discussion. I would not defend including Katz by simply pointing to the three-name limit.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B006 first. He argues that Autor and Hanson are central to the trade-shock and task evidence and Katz to the skill-demand literature, and that Dorn is an important but more junior co-author. He also asks whether the committee sees one coherent discovery or two separate lines.
responses.response: I agree that the credit pattern favours Autor, Hanson and Katz, but I would not rely on seniority to exclude Dorn. The justification is that Katz and Autor anchor the long-run framework and Hanson anchors the trade-shock design, while Dorn's contribution is real but sits within a strand where two other credited names already carry the design. On his coherence question, I think one citation can hold both strands. Both address how exposure to technology and trade shifts labour demand and distributes adjustment costs. The citation should therefore be framed around labour-demand adjustment, not around either channel alone.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B004 second. He notes that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are the clearest foundational strands but any trio omits major contributors, and that the 2023 and 2024 prizes in labour and technology topics may reduce the marginal case for B006.
responses.response: I agree that B004 attribution is a real weakness. I proposed Taylor, Woodford and Calvo myself and I accept that Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have strong claims. That is the main reason I now prefer B006. On overlap, I think the 2023 and 2024 prizes covered a different question: gender gaps in labour markets and institutions as determinants of prosperity. The task-based account of technology and the import-competition evidence are different questions. I accept that the technology-and-inequality overlap with Acemoglu's recognition is genuine and needs care in the citation.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B032 first and B004 fourth. He regards B004 as intellectually central but with highly diffuse credit and exposure to the post-2008 and 2021–23 inflation challenges. He ranks B006 fifth and says the task-model theory has important contributors outside the credited set.
responses.response: I share the B004 credit concern. I do not see attribution as grounds to rank B006 fifth, though, since the Autor, Hanson and Katz credit map is clearer than any B004 trio. I accept the point about contributors to the task-model theory. That is why I would anchor the citation on the empirical and conceptual account of labour-demand adjustment and not on a claim to have originated the task model. I do not see a stronger contender among the shortlisted macro-finance candidates on maturity and breadth. B032 is a foundational mechanism but has less direct empirical confirmation and a partial overlap with the 2022 prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers Katz, Dorn or a two-name set for B006, and how to word the citation without overclaiming credit for the task framework.
How far the 2023 (Goldin) and 2024 (Acemoglu) prizes overlap with the technology and inequality strand.
Persistence and magnitude of China-shock effects and the shift-share inference concerns.
Whether B004 attribution could be resolved by a narrower pricing-and-policy-rule citation, which would change my ranking.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the shortlisted candidates. My research (matching, auctions, fair allocation) does not overlap with the credited names on any shortlisted ballot. I note collegial links with other committee members as fellow SSE affiliates, and I have co-authored COVID policy work with SSE economists. None of this involves a shortlisted candidate.
